extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsels, PR practitioners, and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations counsel on understanding, influencing, and interacting with public opinion and the media; covers when to conform to or attempt to change established beliefs and how to use channels (press, radio, films, lectures, etc.) effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the a priori judgment of the public
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus the public relations counsel has to consider the a priori judgment of any public he deals with before counseling any step that would modify those things in which the public has an established belief.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before proposing action that would change beliefs, analyze the existing, often instinctive, assumptions of the target public (their 'a priori syntheses' or herd-suggestions) and factor those fixed attitudes into strategy and messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not simply discredit beliefs—discredit authorities or create new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is seldom effective to call names or to attempt to discredit the beliefs themselves... must either discredit the old authorities or create new authorities by making articulate a mass opinion against the old belief or in favor of the new.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than attacking popular beliefs head-on, undermine the credibility of the sources that sustain them or build and publicize new, respected authorities and organized opinion to support the desired change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze whether public opinion is stubborn or malleable
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a divergence of opinion as to whether the public mind is malleable or stubborn—whether it is a passive or an active element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine for each issue and audience whether opinion is likely to resist change or can be shifted; this analysis should guide choice of tactics (education, persuasion, mass campaigns, or accommodation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Map and evaluate the channels that influence public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Many outside forces... go to influence public opinion. The most obvious of these forces are parental influence, the school room, the press, motion pictures, advertising, magazines, lectures, the church, the radio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which institutions and media most shape the target public, and assess their relative power and constraints when planning outreach or persuasion efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilize existing channels to obtain expression for your point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: In view then of the possibility of a malleable public opinion the counsel on public relations, desiring to obtain a hearing for any given cause, simply utilizes existent channels to obtain expression for the point of view he represents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through established media and institutions rather than expecting to create entirely new channels; adapt messaging to the norms and expectations of each channel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the interaction between public and organs (action and reaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Action and interaction are continually going on between the forces projected out to the public and the public itself... The public relations counsel must understand this fact in its broadest and most detailed implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for two‑way dynamics: monitor public response and be ready to adjust messaging or tactics; anticipate feedback loops between media, institutions, and audience behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform to the standards of the organ while appealing to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: It is as important to conform to the standards of the organ which projects ideas as it is to present to this organ such ideas as will conform to the fundamental understanding and appreciation of the public to which they are ultimately to appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn an outlet’s implicit/explicit editorial standards (what it deems 'fit to print', decency limits, privacy concerns) and frame material to pass those filters while still reaching the intended public meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess newsworthiness by timeliness and significance to readers
rubrics_metrics.description: “News,” says he, “is anything timely which is significant to newspaper readers in their relations to the community, the state and the nation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pitching or preparing content, prioritize timeliness and community/national significance; understand that 'significance' is judged relative to the outlet’s readership and may vary widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate editorial censorship and audience-driven omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor... said, ‘Mr. Phillips, that is a very good and interesting letter, and I shall be glad to publish it; but I wish you would consent to strike out the last paragraph.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect editors to delete or reshape material that conflicts with perceived public taste or publisher interests; prepare backups (shorter versions, alternative angles) and decide in advance whether to insist on full publication or accept edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trial balloons and continuous monitoring to test and gauge reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: public statements... were used by the diplomats themselves as a happy means of testing popular opinion... ‘trial balloons’ were sent up... each delegation maintained clipping bureaus... which gave the delegates accurate information as to the state of mind at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ controlled releases, trial statements, and systematic monitoring (press clippings, reactions) to test potential reception and refine strategy before full-scale campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist established points of view rather than oppose them outright
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of any force which attempts to modify public opinion depends upon the success with which it is able to enlist established points of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor new messages to existing beliefs and values where possible; shifting opinion is often easier when new ideas are presented as extensions or reinterpretations of accepted norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use group leaders and sympathetic organizations to legitimize controversial material
rubrics_metrics.description: The producers, therefore, did not try to educate the public by presenting this play as such, but allowed group leaders and groups interested in education to come to the support of Brieux’s drama and, in a sense, to sponsor the production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sensitive topics, recruit credible sponsors, educators, or advocacy groups to endorse or champion the message so it reaches the public as a legitimate, supported initiative rather than as raw provocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run integrated, multi-form campaigns for social change
rubrics_metrics.description: The Safety First movement, by its use of every form of appeal, from poster to circular, from lecture to law enforcement, from motion pictures to ‘safety weeks,’ is bringing about a gradual change...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine posters, print, lectures, films, legal measures, and events to reinforce messages across different contexts and accelerate normative change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint respected public figures or institutions to assure public confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: For like causes we find great industries... appointing as directors of their activities men prominent in public life, doing this to assure the public of the honest and social-minded conduct of their members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prominent, trusted names or institutions on advisory boards or campaigns to lend legitimacy and reassure skeptical audiences about motives and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain accuracy and fairness to secure cooperation from other outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: They realized that the only motive back of the World’s publication was public service... they asked only assurance of its traditional accuracy and fairness before they saw their way clear to coöperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid exaggeration and factual distortion; other media are more likely to syndicate or support material that is demonstrably accurate and presented in good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider public morale and sometimes temper reporting to support community morale
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of any newspaper to realize that there is a possibility of selective action, and that 'in times of stress and bleak despair a newspaper has a hard and fast duty to perform in keeping up the morale of the community.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning publicity in crisis contexts, weigh the social consequences of exposure and consider whether framing, timing, or restraint better serves public interest and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to lead the public by consistent, courageous policy when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: The two Baltimore Suns do brave their public and have been braving their public for some time, not entirely without success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasionally institutions must resist public pressure to uphold principles; sustained, principled consistency can gradually win approval, but this requires commitment and readiness for short-term backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that outlets tailor content to please their audience (commercial motives)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary aim of all of them... was to please the crowd, and to give a good show... and the way they set about giving that good show was by first selecting a deserving victim...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design pitches and campaigns with the outlet’s commercial and audience incentives in mind—sensational or attention-grabbing hooks may be necessary to secure placement, but balance this with long-term credibility.
